title: Doceo
pitch: Teach a website new WebMCP tools by example. Humans demonstrate, agents propose, and the website verifies each workflow before a human approves publication.
about_excerpt: Teach a website new WebMCP tools by example. Humans demonstrate, agents propose, and the website verifies each workflow before a human approves publication. Like Comment Story Updates The learned capability returns a verified cart update. This screenshot shows the local Tool Lab test interface. Three deterministic tests verify the demonstrations and no-match rollback before separate UI approval. Two demonstrations reveal variable inputs and fixed actions, producing a constrained contract. Teach the web by example: demonstrate, compare, verify, and approve a reusable website tool. Inspiration Most websites offer agents only the tools their developers wrote. But users develop useful workflows that were never packaged as tools. That makes us wonder: what if a website could learn a reusable capability from its user, verify what it does, and expose it through WebMCP? Doceo is Latin for “I teach” explores that idea. Its guiding principle is simple: humans demonstrate, agents propose, the website verifies, and lastly humans approve. What it does Doceo turns demonstrated workflows into site-native WebMCP tools. The prototype uses Lumen Market, a demo shopping website. A user demonstrates the same shopping task twice with different searches and budget filters. Doceo records the underlying domain actions not screen coordinates or DOM selectors. Then compares the examples to identify what changes and what stays fixed. An agent can then inspect the evidence, propose a structured tool contract, run isolated tests, and request publication. A separate approval step in the interface registers the tested capability as a new WebMCP tool. The resulting find_and_add_product tool accepts new inputs, selects a matching product, and updates the same cart visible to the user. If execution fails its checks, the interpreter restores the previous state. The important transition is not simply from clicks to automation. It is from demonstrated intent to a verified capability on the website’s own tool surface. How I built it The application uses React, TypeScript, and Vite, with Zod for runtime contract validation. Doceo exposes four WebMCP meta-tools: get_workflow_evidence propose_tool_contract run_candidate_tests request_tool_publish These let an agent participate in tool creation before the learned tool exists. Proposed contracts use a constrained intermediate representation backed by five allowlisted domain actions. They cannot introduce arbitrary JavaScript. A deterministic interpreter executes those actions and checks their observable effects. Verification covers the recorded demonstrations and a no-match safety case. Editing a contract invalidates its previous test results, and approval reruns verification against the current evidence. Sessions persist across reloads, evidence and contracts can be exported, and published tools can be revoked. Parallel AI supported project and technical research during development. Graphify supported codebase navigation and persistent project context. Neither is required to execute the demo’s learned tools. Challenges I ran into The hardest problem was deciding what the examples actually justify. Two demonstrations can suggest a reusable pattern, but they do not prove a user’s general intent. Doceo therefore keeps its scope narrow, exposes the proposed contract for review, and rejects incompatible demonstrations. Another challenge was separating proposal from publication. The WebMCP publication tool only requests approval; registration happens through a separate interface action after verification. It was also important to distinguish compatibility testing from native integration. A local test harness is useful, but it is not evidence that native WebMCP discovery and invocation work. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The prototype completes the full demonstrate --> propose --> verify --> approve --> invoke cycle. Native WebMCP testing confirmed discovery of the four meta-tools, runtime appearance of the approved fifth tool, successful invocation, and removal after revocation. The current automated suite passes 16 unit tests and 9 end-to-end tests, including persistence, contract editing, rollback, responsive layouts, and automated accessibility checks. What I learned Recording behavior is easier than establishing a trustworthy contract for repeating it. Stable domain actions, explicit parameters, observable postconditions, and reversible execution matter more than a convincing replay. I also learned that WebMCP can support more than a fixed integration: it can provide the interface through which an agent helps a website construct and validate a new capability. What's next for Doceo The next steps are a public deployment, a reproducible demo, and evaluation with additional users and workflows. I also want to add clarification questions when demonstrations are ambiguous and compare agent-assisted execution against UI-only execution using measured success rates, latency, and token usage. The current prototype is intentionally limited to an instrumented shopping website. It does not claim to learn arbitrary workflows on arbitrary websites. The longer-term goal is a reusable teaching layer that other websites can adopt while retaining control over their actions, verification rules, and publication decisions. video_transcript_excerpt: I begin by demonstrating a real task on Lumen Market. I search for a desk lamp, set a maximum price of $100, and add the matching product to the bag. Then I repeat the same workflow with different values. A task light under $70. With two demonstrations captured, the foundry compares them. The search query and maximum price change, so they become tool inputs. Quantity stays fixed at one. The recorded product ID also changes, but it is an outcome, not a useful input. Now I hand the page to the WebMCP enabled agent. It reads the evidence directly from the website and finds 100% sequence agreement across four domain actions. The agent proposes a constrained contract named find and add product. Instead of hard-coding either recorded item, the contract uses semantic best match selection. It contains only approved site actions, never arbitrary generated JavaScript. Docio runs three isolated tests. Both recorded workflows produce the expected card effects. A separate safety test deliberately searches for a product that does not exist. The operation is rejected, and the complete state is rolled back. All three tests pass. The agent may request publication, but it cannot approve itself. I review the contract and publish the tool with an explicit human click. Thus, the browser now exposes find and add product as a new WebMCP capability at runtime. To prove that this is a reusable tool rather than a replay, I ask the agent for something never shown in the demonstrations, a wall clock under $110. The learned tool finds the Dawn wall clock for $96 and adds one to the demo cart. The structured tool result in the visible website state confirm the same outcome without the agent clicking the interface. Finally, I revoke the learned tool. The agent refreshes the page's web MCP capabilities and confirms that it has disappeared from both the tool lab and the browser tool list. Docu CEO shows how people and agents can grow a website's capabilities together.
